statement: This question investigates formulae for the sums of powers of the first $n$ positive integers. For $k \in \mathbb{N}$ and $n \in \mathbb{Z}^+$ let $$S_k(n)=\sum_{r=1}^{n} r^k = 1^k+2^k+\cdots+n^k.$$ (a) Write down an expression for $S_0(n)$, and find the values of $S_1(4)$, $S_2(4)$ and $S_3(4)$. [2] (b) By considering $\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left[(r+1)^2-r^2\right]$ in two different ways, show that $S_1(n)=\dfrac{n(n+1)}{2}$. [3] (c) (i) Expand and simplify $(r+1)^3-r^3$. (ii) By summing both sides of your answer to part (c)(i) from $r=1$ to $r=n$, show that $3S_2(n)=(n+1)^3-1-3S_1(n)-n$. (iii) Hence show that $S_2(n)=\dfrac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6}$. [6] (d) Prove by mathematical induction that $S_3(n)=\left(\dfrac{n(n+1)}{2}\right)^2$ for all $n \in \mathbb{Z}^+$. [6] (e) The results so far suggest that $S_k(n)$ is a polynomial in $n$ of degree $k+1$ with leading coefficient $\dfrac{1}{k+1}$. (i) Verify this conjecture for $k=1$, $k=2$ and $k=3$ by expanding your formulae. (ii) By considering $\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left[(r+1)^{k+1}-r^{k+1}\right]$ and the binomial theorem, explain why the conjecture is true for every $k \in \mathbb{Z}^+$. [5] (f) By writing $\dfrac{S_k(n)}{n^{k+1}}=\dfrac{1}{n}\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(\dfrac{r}{n}\right)^k$, interpret this quantity as an approximation to a definite integral, and hence find $\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{S_k(n)}{n^{k+1}}$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $S_0(n)=n$ [A1] $S_1(4)=10,\ S_2(4)=30,\ S_3(4)=100$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) Telescoping: $\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left[(r+1)^2-r^2\right]=(n+1)^2-1$ [M1] Expanding instead: $\sum_{r=1}^{n}(2r+1)=2S_1(n)+n$ [A1] so $2S_1(n)=n^2+2n-n=n^2+n$, giving $S_1(n)=\dfrac{n(n+1)}{2}$ [A1][AG] [3 marks] (c)(i) $(r+1)^3-r^3=3r^2+3r+1$ [A1] (ii) The left-hand side telescopes to $(n+1)^3-1$ [M1]; the right-hand side sums to $3S_2(n)+3S_1(n)+n$ [A1], which rearranges to the given result [AG] (iii) $3S_2(n)=(n+1)^3-(n+1)-\dfrac{3n(n+1)}{2}$ [M1] $=n(n+1)(n+2)-\dfrac{3n(n+1)}{2}=\dfrac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{2}$ [A1] so $S_2(n)=\dfrac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6}$ [A1][AG] [6 marks] (d) For $n=1$: LHS $=1$, RHS $=\left(\frac{1\cdot 2}{2}\right)^2=1$, so true for $n=1$ [A1] Assume true for $n=m$, i.e. $S_3(m)=\dfrac{m^2(m+1)^2}{4}$ [M1] Then $S_3(m+1)=\dfrac{m^2(m+1)^2}{4}+(m+1)^3$ [M1] $=\dfrac{(m+1)^2\left(m^2+4m+4\right)}{4}$ [A1] $=\left(\dfrac{(m+1)(m+2)}{2}\right)^2$, which is the statement for $n=m+1$ [A1] Since true for $n=1$, and true for $n=m$ implies true for $n=m+1$, the result holds for all $n\in\mathbb{Z}^+$ by mathematical induction [R1] [6 marks] (e)(i) $S_1=\tfrac12 n^2+\tfrac12 n$, $S_2=\tfrac13 n^3+\tfrac12 n^2+\tfrac16 n$, $S_3=\tfrac14 n^4+\tfrac12 n^3+\tfrac14 n^2$ — each has degree $k+1$ and leading coefficient $\frac{1}{k+1}$ [A2] (award [A1] for two correct) (ii) Telescoping gives $(n+1)^{k+1}-1=\sum_{r=1}^{n}\sum_{j=0}^{k}\binom{k+1}{j}r^j=(k+1)S_k(n)+\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}\binom{k+1}{j}S_j(n)$ [M1] By strong induction on $k$, each $S_j(n)$ with $j<k$ is a polynomial of degree $j+1\le k$, so $(k+1)S_k(n)=(n+1)^{k+1}-(\text{polynomial of degree}\le k)$ [R1] Hence $S_k(n)$ is a polynomial of degree $k+1$ whose leading term is $\dfrac{n^{k+1}}{k+1}$ [A1] [5 marks] (f) $\dfrac{1}{n}\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(\dfrac{r}{n}\right)^k$ is a sum of $n$ rectangles of width $\frac1n$ with heights $f\left(\frac rn\right)$, $f(x)=x^k$: a Riemann sum for $\int_0^1 x^k\,dx$ [M1][R1] so the limit is $\int_0^1 x^k\,dx=\dfrac{1}{k+1}$ [A1] (consistent with (e)) [3 marks] Total [25 marks]
tips: Telescoping sums collapse to first minus last term; for the induction step, factor out (m+1)^2 before expanding.

subtopic: Roots of unity and regular polygons
statement: In this question you will investigate the geometry of the $n$th roots of unity. Let $n \ge 2$ be an integer and let $\omega = e^{\frac{2\pi i}{n}}$. (a) Show that the solutions of $z^n = 1$ are $1, \omega, \omega^2, \ldots, \omega^{n-1}$, and explain why these points are the vertices of a regular $n$-sided polygon inscribed in the unit circle. [3] (b) Show that $1 + \omega + \omega^2 + \cdots + \omega^{n-1} = 0$. [2] (c) Hence show that $\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\cos\frac{2\pi k}{n} = 0$. [2] (d) By factorizing $z^n - 1$ in two ways, show that $$1 + z + z^2 + \cdots + z^{n-1} = \prod_{k=1}^{n-1}\left(z - \omega^k\right).$$ [2] (e) Show that $\left|1-\omega^k\right| = 2\sin\dfrac{k\pi}{n}$ for $k = 1, 2, \ldots, n-1$. [4] (f) The vertex $P_0$ of the polygon is at $1$ and the other vertices are $P_k$ at $\omega^k$. Use parts (d) and (e) to show that the product of the distances $P_0P_1 \times P_0P_2 \times \cdots \times P_0P_{n-1}$ is equal to $n$. [3] (g) Hence show that $\displaystyle\prod_{k=1}^{n-1}\sin\frac{k\pi}{n} = \frac{n}{2^{n-1}}$, and verify this result directly for $n=3$ and $n=4$. [4] (h) (i) For a regular hexagon ($n=6$), find the sum of the squares of the distances from $P_0$ to each of the other five vertices. (ii) Show that, for any $n$, $\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}\left|1-\omega^k\right|^2 = 2n$. [5]
markscheme: (a) Let $z=e^{i\theta}$ ($|z|=1$ since $|z|^n=1$); then $e^{in\theta}=1$ so $n\theta=2\pi k$ [M1] giving $z=e^{\frac{2\pi i k}{n}}=\omega^k$, $k=0,1,\ldots,n-1$, which are $n$ distinct roots [A1] All have modulus $1$ and consecutive arguments differ by $\frac{2\pi}{n}$, so they are equally spaced on the unit circle and form a regular $n$-gon [R1] [3 marks] (b) Geometric series: $\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\omega^k=\frac{1-\omega^n}{1-\omega}$ [M1] $=0$ since $\omega^n=1$ and $\omega\ne 1$ [A1][AG] [2 marks] (c) Taking real parts of (b) [M1] with $\operatorname{Re}\left(\omega^k\right)=\cos\frac{2\pi k}{n}$ [A1] gives $\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\cos\frac{2\pi k}{n}=0$ [AG] [2 marks] (d) The roots of $z^n-1$ are $\omega^k$, so $z^n-1=\prod_{k=0}^{n-1}\left(z-\omega^k\right)=(z-1)\prod_{k=1}^{n-1}\left(z-\omega^k\right)$ [M1] Also $z^n-1=(z-1)\left(1+z+\cdots+z^{n-1}\right)$; comparing (polynomial identity) gives the result [A1][AG] [2 marks] (e) With $\theta=\frac{2\pi k}{n}$: $1-\omega^k=(1-\cos\theta)-i\sin\theta$ [M1] $\left|1-\omega^k\right|^2=(1-\cos\theta)^2+\sin^2\theta=2-2\cos\theta$ [A1] $=4\sin^2\frac{\theta}{2}=4\sin^2\frac{k\pi}{n}$ [A1] Since $0<\frac{k\pi}{n}<\pi$, $\sin\frac{k\pi}{n}>0$, so $\left|1-\omega^k\right|=2\sin\frac{k\pi}{n}$ [R1][AG] [4 marks] (f) Substituting $z=1$ in (d) (valid as it is a polynomial identity): $\prod_{k=1}^{n-1}\left(1-\omega^k\right)=n$ [M1][A1] Taking moduli, $\prod_{k=1}^{n-1}P_0P_k=\prod_{k=1}^{n-1}\left|1-\omega^k\right|=n$ [R1][AG] [3 marks] (g) Using (e): $2^{n-1}\prod_{k=1}^{n-1}\sin\frac{k\pi}{n}=n$, so the product is $\frac{n}{2^{n-1}}$ [A1] $n=3$: $\sin\frac{\pi}{3}\sin\frac{2\pi}{3}=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\cdot\frac{\sqrt3}{2}=\frac34=\frac{3}{2^2}$ [A1][A1] $n=4$: $\sin\frac{\pi}{4}\sin\frac{\pi}{2}\sin\frac{3\pi}{4}=\frac{\sqrt2}{2}\cdot1\cdot\frac{\sqrt2}{2}=\frac12=\frac{4}{2^3}$ [A1] [4 marks] (h)(i) Distances are $2\sin\frac{k\pi}{6}$: $1,\sqrt3,2,\sqrt3,1$, so the sum of squares is $1+3+4+3+1=12$ [A1] (ii) $\left|1-\omega^k\right|^2=2-2\cos\frac{2\pi k}{n}$ [M1] so the sum is $2(n-1)-2\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}\cos\frac{2\pi k}{n}$ [M1] From (c), $\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}\cos\frac{2\pi k}{n}=-1$ (removing the $k=0$ term) [A1] so the sum is $2(n-1)+2=2n$ [A1][AG] [5 marks] Total [25 marks]
tips: Keep the identity in (d) as a polynomial identity so you may substitute z = 1 afterwards.

statement: This question investigates ratios of consecutive terms in sequences defined by recurrence relations. The sequence $\{u_n\}$ is defined by $u_1 = 1$, $u_2 = 1$ and $u_{n+2} = u_{n+1} + u_n$ for $n \ge 1$. (a) Write down the values of $u_3, u_4, \ldots, u_8$. [2] (b) Let $r_n = \dfrac{u_{n+1}}{u_n}$. Calculate $r_1, r_2, \ldots, r_7$, giving non-integer answers to four significant figures, and describe the behavior of $r_n$. [3] (c) Show that $r_{n+1} = 1 + \dfrac{1}{r_n}$. [2] (d) Assuming that $\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty} r_n = L$ exists, show that $L = \dfrac{1+\sqrt5}{2}$. [3] (e) Let $\varphi = \dfrac{1+\sqrt5}{2}$ and $\psi = \dfrac{1-\sqrt5}{2}$. (i) Show that $\varphi^2 = \varphi + 1$ and $\psi^2 = \psi + 1$. (ii) Prove by mathematical induction that $u_n = \dfrac{\varphi^n - \psi^n}{\sqrt5}$ for all $n \in \mathbb{Z}^+$. [7] (f) Use the result from part (e) to prove that $\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty} r_n = \varphi$, without assuming that the limit exists. [4] (g) Now consider the sequence $v_1 = 1$, $v_2 = 1$, $v_{n+2} = v_{n+1} + k\,v_n$, where $k > 0$. Assuming that $\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{v_{n+1}}{v_n}$ exists, find this limit in terms of $k$, and find the value of $k$ for which the limit is $2$. [4]
markscheme: (a) $2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21$ [A2] (award [A1] for at least four correct) [2 marks] (b) $r_1=1,\ r_2=2,\ r_3=1.5,\ r_4=1.667,\ r_5=1.6,\ r_6=1.625,\ r_7=1.615$ [A2] (award [A1] for at least four correct) The ratios alternate above and below a value, with the oscillations decreasing in size: they appear to converge to approximately $1.618$ [R1] [3 marks] (c) $r_{n+1}=\dfrac{u_{n+2}}{u_{n+1}}=\dfrac{u_{n+1}+u_n}{u_{n+1}}$ [M1] $=1+\dfrac{u_n}{u_{n+1}}=1+\dfrac{1}{r_n}$ [A1][AG] [2 marks] (d) Letting $n\to\infty$: $L=1+\dfrac1L$ [M1] so $L^2-L-1=0$ and $L=\dfrac{1\pm\sqrt5}{2}$ [A1] Since $r_n>0$ for all $n$, $L\ge0$, so $L=\dfrac{1+\sqrt5}{2}$ [R1][AG] [3 marks] (e)(i) $\varphi^2=\dfrac{6+2\sqrt5}{4}=\dfrac{3+\sqrt5}{2}=\varphi+1$ [A1] and similarly $\psi^2=\dfrac{3-\sqrt5}{2}=\psi+1$ [A1] (ii) $n=1$: $\dfrac{\varphi-\psi}{\sqrt5}=\dfrac{\sqrt5}{\sqrt5}=1=u_1$; $n=2$: $\dfrac{\varphi^2-\psi^2}{\sqrt5}=\dfrac{(\varphi-\psi)(\varphi+\psi)}{\sqrt5}=1\times1=1=u_2$ [A1] Assume the formula holds for $n=m$ and $n=m+1$ [M1] Then $u_{m+2}=u_{m+1}+u_m=\dfrac{\varphi^m(\varphi+1)-\psi^m(\psi+1)}{\sqrt5}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{\varphi^m\varphi^2-\psi^m\psi^2}{\sqrt5}=\dfrac{\varphi^{m+2}-\psi^{m+2}}{\sqrt5}$ using (i) [A1] Since true for $n=1,2$, and truth for $n=m$ and $n=m+1$ implies truth for $n=m+2$, the formula holds for all $n\in\mathbb{Z}^+$ by induction [R1] [7 marks] (f) $r_n=\dfrac{\varphi^{n+1}-\psi^{n+1}}{\varphi^n-\psi^n}$ [M1] $=\varphi\cdot\dfrac{1-\left(\psi/\varphi\right)^{n+1}}{1-\left(\psi/\varphi\right)^{n}}$ [A1] $\left|\dfrac{\psi}{\varphi}\right|=\dfrac{\sqrt5-1}{\sqrt5+1}\approx0.382<1$, so $\left(\dfrac{\psi}{\varphi}\right)^n\to0$ [R1] Hence $r_n\to\varphi$ [A1] [4 marks] (g) $w_n=\dfrac{v_{n+1}}{v_n}$ satisfies $w_{n+1}=1+\dfrac{k}{w_n}$, so the limit $M$ satisfies $M=1+\dfrac{k}{M}$ [M1] $M^2-M-k=0$ [A1] $M=\dfrac{1+\sqrt{1+4k}}{2}$ (positive root since $v_n>0$) [A1] $M=2\Rightarrow 4-2-k=0\Rightarrow k=2$ [A1] [4 marks] Total [25 marks]
tips: Two base cases are needed because the recurrence uses the two previous terms.

statement: This question investigates the family of integrals $$I_n = \int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \sin^n x \, dx, \qquad n \in \mathbb{N}.$$ (a) Find the exact values of $I_0$ and $I_1$. [2] (b) By writing $\sin^n x = \sin^{n-1}x \sin x$ and using integration by parts, show that $I_n = \dfrac{n-1}{n} I_{n-2}$ for $n \ge 2$. [6] (c) Hence find the exact values of $I_2$, $I_3$, $I_4$ and $I_5$. [3] (d) Show that $n I_n I_{n-1} = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$ for all $n \ge 1$. [4] (e) Explain why $I_{n+1} \le I_n \le I_{n-1}$ for $n \ge 1$. [2] (f) Using parts (b) and (e), show that $\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{I_n}{I_{n-1}} = 1$. [3] (g) Use parts (d) and (f) to show that $\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty} n I_n^2 = \frac{\pi}{2}$. Hence write down an approximation for $I_n$ when $n$ is large, and use it to estimate $I_{100}$ to three significant figures. [5]
markscheme: (a) $I_0=\int_0^{\pi/2}1\,dx=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ [A1] $I_1=\left[-\cos x\right]_0^{\pi/2}=1$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) Let $u=\sin^{n-1}x$, $\dfrac{dv}{dx}=\sin x$ [M1] so $\dfrac{du}{dx}=(n-1)\sin^{n-2}x\cos x$, $v=-\cos x$ [A1] $I_n=\left[-\sin^{n-1}x\cos x\right]_0^{\pi/2}+(n-1)\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin^{n-2}x\cos^2x\,dx$ [A1] The boundary term is $0$ at both limits (as $n\ge2$) [R1] Using $\cos^2x=1-\sin^2x$: $I_n=(n-1)\left(I_{n-2}-I_n\right)$ [M1] so $nI_n=(n-1)I_{n-2}$, i.e. $I_n=\dfrac{n-1}{n}I_{n-2}$ [A1][AG] [6 marks] (c) $I_2=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$, $I_3=\dfrac23$ [A1] $I_4=\dfrac34\cdot\dfrac{\pi}{4}=\dfrac{3\pi}{16}$ [A1] $I_5=\dfrac45\cdot\dfrac23=\dfrac{8}{15}$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) For $n=1$: $1\cdot I_1I_0=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ [A1] For $n\ge2$: $nI_nI_{n-1}=n\cdot\dfrac{n-1}{n}I_{n-2}I_{n-1}$ [M1] $=(n-1)I_{n-1}I_{n-2}$ [A1] so the quantity $nI_nI_{n-1}$ does not depend on $n$; by induction it equals $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ for all $n\ge1$ [R1] [4 marks] (e) For $0\le x\le\frac{\pi}{2}$, $0\le\sin x\le1$, so $\sin^{n+1}x\le\sin^nx\le\sin^{n-1}x$ [R1] Integrating an inequality over $\left[0,\frac{\pi}{2}\right]$ preserves it [R1] [2 marks] (f) Dividing by $I_{n-1}>0$: $\dfrac{I_{n+1}}{I_{n-1}}\le\dfrac{I_n}{I_{n-1}}\le1$ [M1] By (b), $\dfrac{I_{n+1}}{I_{n-1}}=\dfrac{n}{n+1}\to1$ [A1] so by the squeeze principle $\dfrac{I_n}{I_{n-1}}\to1$ [R1] [3 marks] (g) $nI_n^2=\left(nI_nI_{n-1}\right)\cdot\dfrac{I_n}{I_{n-1}}$ [M1] $=\dfrac{\pi}{2}\cdot\dfrac{I_n}{I_{n-1}}$ [A1] $\to\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ by (f) [R1] So $I_n\approx\sqrt{\dfrac{\pi}{2n}}$ [A1] $I_{100}\approx\sqrt{\dfrac{\pi}{200}}\approx0.125$ [A1] [5 marks] Total [25 marks]
tips: In (b) the boundary term vanishes because sin 0 = 0 and cos(π/2) = 0.

statement: This question investigates models for the population of fish in a lake. Let $P$ be the number of fish, in thousands, $t$ years after the lake was first stocked with $2000$ fish. (a) In model A, $\dfrac{dP}{dt} = 0.4P$. (i) Solve this differential equation to find $P$ in terms of $t$. (ii) Find the number of fish predicted by model A after $10$ years. (iii) State one reason why model A is unrealistic in the long term. [4] In model B, $\dfrac{dP}{dt} = 0.4P\left(1 - \dfrac{P}{20}\right)$. (b) (i) Find the equilibrium values of $P$ for model B. (ii) Find the value of $P$ for which the population grows fastest, and the maximum rate of growth. [5] (c) Show that $P = \dfrac{20}{1 + 9e^{-0.4t}}$ satisfies the differential equation in model B and the initial condition. [5] (d) Using model B, find the time taken for the population to reach $15\,000$ fish. [3] (e) A fishing company proposes to harvest fish at a constant rate of $h$ thousand fish per year, so that $\dfrac{dP}{dt} = 0.4P\left(1 - \dfrac{P}{20}\right) - h$. (i) For $h = 1.5$, find the equilibrium values of $P$ and determine whether each is stable or unstable. (ii) Find the largest value of $h$ for which the population can be maintained at a constant level. [6] (f) Use Euler's method with a step length of $0.5$ to estimate $P(1)$ for model B (without harvesting). Compare your answer with the exact value from part (c) and explain the difference. [4]
markscheme: (a)(i) $\displaystyle\int\frac{dP}{P}=\int0.4\,dt\Rightarrow\ln P=0.4t+c$ [M1] $P=2e^{0.4t}$ [A1] (ii) $P(10)=2e^{4}=109.196\ldots$, so about $109\,000$ fish [A1] (iii) e.g. it predicts unlimited growth, but the lake has limited food/space [R1] [4 marks] (b)(i) $P=0$ and $P=20$ [A1][A1] (ii) $\dfrac{dP}{dt}=0.4P-0.02P^2$ is a quadratic in $P$, maximized where $0.4-0.04P=0$ [M1] $P=10$ (i.e. $10\,000$ fish) [A1] maximum rate $=0.4\times10\times0.5=2$ thousand fish per year [A1] [5 marks] (c) $P(0)=\dfrac{20}{1+9}=2$ [A1] $\dfrac{dP}{dt}=\dfrac{20\times9\times0.4e^{-0.4t}}{\left(1+9e^{-0.4t}\right)^2}=\dfrac{72e^{-0.4t}}{\left(1+9e^{-0.4t}\right)^2}$ [M1][A1] $1-\dfrac{P}{20}=1-\dfrac{1}{1+9e^{-0.4t}}=\dfrac{9e^{-0.4t}}{1+9e^{-0.4t}}$ [A1] so $0.4P\left(1-\dfrac{P}{20}\right)=0.4\cdot\dfrac{20}{1+9e^{-0.4t}}\cdot\dfrac{9e^{-0.4t}}{1+9e^{-0.4t}}=\dfrac{72e^{-0.4t}}{\left(1+9e^{-0.4t}\right)^2}=\dfrac{dP}{dt}$ [A1][AG] [5 marks] (d) $\dfrac{20}{1+9e^{-0.4t}}=15$ [M1] $e^{-0.4t}=\dfrac{1}{27}$ [A1] $t=\dfrac{\ln27}{0.4}=8.24$ years [A1] [3 marks] (e)(i) $0.4P-0.02P^2-1.5=0\Rightarrow P^2-20P+75=0$ [M1] $P=5$ or $P=15$ [A1] Let $f(P)=0.4P\left(1-\frac{P}{20}\right)-1.5$: $f(P)<0$ for $P<5$, $f(P)>0$ for $5<P<15$, $f(P)<0$ for $P>15$ (or $f'(5)=0.2>0$, $f'(15)=-0.2<0$) [R1] so $P=15$ is stable and $P=5$ is unstable [A1] (ii) An equilibrium exists only if $h\le$ the maximum of $0.4P\left(1-\frac{P}{20}\right)$ [M1] so $h_{\max}=2$, i.e. $2000$ fish per year [A1] [6 marks] (f) $P_{n+1}=P_n+0.5\times0.4P_n\left(1-\frac{P_n}{20}\right)$ [M1] $P(0.5)\approx2+0.5\times0.72=2.36$ [A1] $P(1)\approx2.36+0.5\times0.832608=2.78$ [A1] Exact value $\dfrac{20}{1+9e^{-0.4}}=2.84$; Euler underestimates because the solution curve is concave up for $P<10$, so the tangent lies below the curve [R1] [4 marks] Total [27 marks]
tips: For stability, check the sign of dP/dt on either side of each equilibrium.

statement: A bike-share scheme has three docking stations, $A$, $B$ and $C$. Bikes are moved by customers during the day and every bike is docked at one of the stations each night. Records show that, from one night to the next: of the bikes at $A$, $50\%$ stay at $A$, $10\%$ move to $B$ and $40\%$ move to $C$; of the bikes at $B$, $20\%$ move to $A$, $60\%$ stay at $B$ and $20\%$ move to $C$; of the bikes at $C$, $30\%$ move to $A$, $10\%$ move to $B$ and $60\%$ stay at $C$. On the first night there are $200$ bikes at $A$, $150$ at $B$ and $150$ at $C$. Let $\mathbf{s}_n$ be the column vector giving the numbers of bikes at $A$, $B$, $C$ after $n$ days, so that $\mathbf{s}_0 = \begin{pmatrix}200\\150\\150\end{pmatrix}$. (a) Write down the transition matrix $T$ such that $\mathbf{s}_{n+1} = T\mathbf{s}_n$. [2] (b) Find $\mathbf{s}_1$ and $\mathbf{s}_3$. [3] (c) Find the probability that a bike that is at $B$ tonight will be at $A$ two nights later. [2] (d) (i) Verify that $\begin{pmatrix}1\\-3\\2\end{pmatrix}$ and $\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\\-1\end{pmatrix}$ are eigenvectors of $T$, and state the corresponding eigenvalues. (ii) Show that $\begin{pmatrix}7\\4\\9\end{pmatrix}$ is an eigenvector of $T$ with eigenvalue $1$. [5] (e) By writing $\mathbf{s}_0$ as a linear combination of the three eigenvectors, find an expression for $\mathbf{s}_n$, and hence show that the number of bikes at $A$ after $n$ days is $$175 - \frac{50}{3}(0.5)^n + \frac{125}{3}(0.2)^n.$$ [6] (f) Write down the long-term number of bikes at each station. [2] (g) Find the first day on which the number of bikes at $B$ is within $1$ of its long-term value. [3] (h) The company wants at least $120$ bikes to be at $B$ in the long term. Assuming the same transition probabilities, find the minimum number of extra bikes that should be added to the scheme. [2]
markscheme: (a) $T=\begin{pmatrix}0.5&0.2&0.3\\0.1&0.6&0.1\\0.4&0.2&0.6\end{pmatrix}$ [A2] (award [A1] for the transpose or one column incorrect) [2 marks] (b) $\mathbf{s}_1=T\mathbf{s}_0=\begin{pmatrix}175\\125\\200\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] $\mathbf{s}_3=T^3\mathbf{s}_0$ [M1] $=\begin{pmatrix}173.25\\106.25\\220.5\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $T^2=\begin{pmatrix}0.39&0.28&0.35\\0.15&0.40&0.15\\0.46&0.32&0.50\end{pmatrix}$ [M1] the required entry (row $A$, column $B$) is $0.28$ [A1] [2 marks] (d)(i) $T\begin{pmatrix}1\\-3\\2\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}0.5\\-1.5\\1\end{pmatrix}=0.5\begin{pmatrix}1\\-3\\2\end{pmatrix}$ [M1][A1] $T\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\\-1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}0.2\\0\\-0.2\end{pmatrix}=0.2\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\\-1\end{pmatrix}$ [A1] (ii) $T\begin{pmatrix}7\\4\\9\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}3.5+0.8+2.7\\0.7+2.4+0.9\\2.8+0.8+5.4\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}7\\4\\9\end{pmatrix}$ [M1][A1][AG] [5 marks] (e) $\mathbf{s}_0=a\begin{pmatrix}7\\4\\9\end{pmatrix}+b\begin{pmatrix}1\\-3\\2\end{pmatrix}+c\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\\-1\end{pmatrix}$ [M1] Adding the three equations gives $20a=500$, so $a=25$; then $4a-3b=150\Rightarrow b=-\dfrac{50}{3}$; $7a+b+c=200\Rightarrow c=\dfrac{125}{3}$ [A1][A1][A1] $\mathbf{s}_n=T^n\mathbf{s}_0=25\begin{pmatrix}7\\4\\9\end{pmatrix}-\dfrac{50}{3}(0.5)^n\begin{pmatrix}1\\-3\\2\end{pmatrix}+\dfrac{125}{3}(0.2)^n\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\\-1\end{pmatrix}$ [M1] First component: $175-\dfrac{50}{3}(0.5)^n+\dfrac{125}{3}(0.2)^n$ [A1][AG] [6 marks] (f) As $n\to\infty$, $(0.5)^n\to0$ and $(0.2)^n\to0$: $A=175$, $B=100$, $C=225$ [A2] [2 marks] (g) $B_n=100+50(0.5)^n$ [A1] $50(0.5)^n<1\Rightarrow n>\dfrac{\ln 50}{\ln 2}=5.64$ [M1] so after $6$ days [A1] [3 marks] (h) Long-term proportion at $B$ is $\dfrac{4}{20}=0.2$, so the total must be at least $\dfrac{120}{0.2}=600$ [M1] i.e. $100$ extra bikes [A1] [2 marks] Total [25 marks]
tips: Columns of a transition matrix (used as T s_n) sum to 1; eigenvectors for eigenvalues other than 1 have components summing to 0.

subtopic: Route inspection, spanning trees and TSP
statement: A water company maintains pipes between six pumping stations, $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$, $E$ and $F$. The lengths of the pipes, in kilometers, are listed in this weighted adjacency table, where a dash means there is no direct pipe. $$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline & A & B & C & D & E & F \\ \hline A & - & 7 & 4 & 9 & - & - \\ \hline B & 7 & - & 3 & - & 6 & - \\ \hline C & 4 & 3 & - & 5 & 8 & 11 \\ \hline D & 9 & - & 5 & - & 4 & 7 \\ \hline E & - & 6 & 8 & 4 & - & 5 \\ \hline F & - & - & 11 & 7 & 5 & - \\ \hline\end{array}$$ (a) Draw a weighted graph $G$ to represent this information. [2] (b) State, with a reason, whether $G$ has an Eulerian circuit. [2] (c) Use Kruskal's algorithm to find a minimum spanning tree for $G$. List the edges in the order in which they are added and state the total length of the tree. [4] (d) Use Dijkstra's algorithm to find the shortest route from $A$ to $F$, and state its length. [4] (e) An inspector must travel along every pipe at least once, starting and finishing at $A$. (i) Find the total length of all the pipes. (ii) By considering all possible pairings of the odd vertices, find the length of the shortest possible inspection route, and state which pipes must be traveled twice. [6] (f) An engineer must visit every station, starting and finishing at $A$. (i) Construct the table of least distances between every pair of stations. (ii) Use the nearest neighbor algorithm, starting at $A$, to find an upper bound for the length of the engineer's route. (iii) By deleting vertex $A$, use the deleted vertex algorithm to find a lower bound for the length of the route. (iv) The route $A\,B\,E\,F\,D\,C\,A$ has length $34$ km. Explain what can be concluded about the optimal route. [12]
markscheme: (a) Graph with vertices $A$–$F$ and the eleven weighted edges $AB=7$, $AC=4$, $AD=9$, $BC=3$, $BE=6$, $CD=5$, $CE=8$, $CF=11$, $DE=4$, $DF=7$, $EF=5$ [A2] (award [A1] for one omission or error) [2 marks] (b) The degrees are $A:3,\ B:3,\ C:5,\ D:4,\ E:4,\ F:3$ [A1] Since there are vertices of odd degree, $G$ has no Eulerian circuit [R1] [2 marks] (c) $BC\,(3)$, $AC\,(4)$, $DE\,(4)$, $CD\,(5)$, $EF\,(5)$ [M1][A2] (award [A1] for correct edges in an incorrect order, or $AC$/$DE$ in either order is fine) total length $21$ km [A1] [4 marks] (d) Correct labeling from $A$: $C=4$, $B=7$, $D=9$, $E=12$, $F=15$ [M1][A1] shortest route $A\,C\,F$ [A1] length $15$ km [A1] [4 marks] (e)(i) $7+4+9+3+6+5+8+11+4+7+5=69$ km [A1] (ii) Odd vertices: $A, B, C, F$ [A1] Pairings: $AB+CF=7+11=18$; $AC+BF=4+11=15$; $AF+BC=15+3=18$ [M1][A1] Minimum is $AC+BF=15$, where the shortest $B$ to $F$ route is $B\,E\,F$ [A1] Route length $69+15=84$ km, repeating pipes $AC$, $BE$ and $EF$ [A1] [6 marks] (f)(i) $$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline & A & B & C & D & E & F \\ \hline A & - & 7 & 4 & 9 & 12 & 15 \\ \hline B & 7 & - & 3 & 8 & 6 & 11 \\ \hline C & 4 & 3 & - & 5 & 8 & 11 \\ \hline D & 9 & 8 & 5 & - & 4 & 7 \\ \hline E & 12 & 6 & 8 & 4 & - & 5 \\ \hline F & 15 & 11 & 11 & 7 & 5 & - \\ \hline\end{array}$$ [A3] (award [A2] for one or two errors, [A1] for three or four errors) (ii) $A\to C\,(4)\to B\,(3)\to E\,(6)\to D\,(4)\to F\,(7)\to A\,(15)$ [M1][A1] upper bound $=39$ km [A1] (iii) Minimum spanning tree of $B, C, D, E, F$: $BC\,(3)$, $DE\,(4)$, $CD\,(5)$, $EF\,(5)$, weight $17$ [M1][A1] add the two shortest edges from $A$: $4+7=11$ [M1] lower bound $=28$ km [A1] (iv) $34$ km is a better (lower) upper bound than $39$ km [R1] so the optimal route length $L$ satisfies $28\le L\le34$ [A1] [12 marks] Total [30 marks]
tips: For the traveling salesman parts, always work from the table of least distances, not the original table.

statement: A teacher investigates whether the time students spend revising is related to their test scores. Eight students recorded the number of hours, $x$, they spent revising and their test score, $y$ (out of $100$). $$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline x & 2 & 3 & 5 & 6 & 8 & 9 & 11 & 12 \\ \hline y & 48 & 50 & 59 & 61 & 70 & 68 & 80 & 84 \\ \hline\end{array}$$ (a) Calculate Pearson's product-moment correlation coefficient, $r$, and interpret its value. [3] (b) Find the equation of the regression line of $y$ on $x$. [2] (c) (i) Use your regression line to estimate the score of a student who revised for $7$ hours. (ii) Explain why it would not be appropriate to use the line to estimate the score of a student who revised for $20$ hours. [3] (d) Test, at the $1\%$ significance level, whether there is positive correlation between $x$ and $y$ in the population. State your hypotheses, the $p$-value and your conclusion. [5] (e) (i) Calculate Spearman's rank correlation coefficient, $r_s$, for the data. (ii) Explain why $r_s$ is slightly smaller than $1$ even though $y$ generally increases with $x$. [4] The teacher then surveys $100$ students about their main revision method and whether they passed the test. $$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|}\hline \text{Method} & \text{Pass} & \text{Fail} \\ \hline \text{Flashcards} & 18 & 12 \\ \hline \text{Past papers} & 27 & 8 \\ \hline \text{Re-reading notes} & 15 & 20 \\ \hline\end{array}$$ (f) Perform a $\chi^2$ test for independence at the $5\%$ significance level. State your hypotheses, the expected frequencies, the number of degrees of freedom, the $\chi^2$ statistic, the $p$-value and your conclusion. [7] (g) State, with a reason, whether your conclusion to part (f) would change at the $1\%$ significance level. [1]
markscheme: (a) $r=0.990$ (to 3 s.f.) [A2] very strong positive linear correlation [R1] [3 marks] (b) $y=3.55x+40.1$ (more precisely $y=3.554x+40.12$) [A1][A1] [2 marks] (c)(i) $y=3.554\times7+40.12\approx65.0$ [A1] (ii) $20$ hours is outside the range of the data ($2\le x\le12$), so this is extrapolation [R1]; also the line predicts about $111$, which exceeds the maximum score of $100$ [R1] [3 marks] (d) $H_0:\ \rho=0$; $H_1:\ \rho>0$ [A1][A1] $p$-value $=1.26\times10^{-6}$ (from $t=17.1$ with $6$ degrees of freedom) [A1] since $p<0.01$ [R1] reject $H_0$: there is evidence of positive correlation between revision time and score [A1] [5 marks] (e)(i) ranks of $x$: $1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8$; ranks of $y$: $1,2,3,4,6,5,7,8$ [M1] $\sum d^2=2$, $r_s=1-\dfrac{6\times2}{8\times63}=0.976$ [A1][A1] (ii) the relationship is not perfectly monotonic: the student with $x=9$ scored less than the student with $x=8$ [R1] [4 marks] (f) $H_0$: pass/fail is independent of revision method; $H_1$: pass/fail is not independent of revision method [A1] Expected frequencies: Flashcards $18, 12$; Past papers $21, 14$; Re-reading $21, 14$ [A1] degrees of freedom $=(3-1)(2-1)=2$ [A1] $\chi^2=8.57$ [A1] $p$-value $=0.0138$ [A1] since $0.0138<0.05$ [R1] reject $H_0$: there is evidence that the result depends on the revision method [A1] [7 marks] (g) Yes: $0.0138>0.01$, so at the $1\%$ level $H_0$ would not be rejected [R1] [1 mark] Total [25 marks]
tips: State hypotheses in terms of the population parameter (ρ), not the sample value r.
